scenes.visual: Title card: Plant Signals Steer Growth. Show a shoot bending toward light and a horizontal seedling with its shoot curving up and root down. No experimental apparatus.

scenes.tts: Light an oat seedling from one side, and its shoot bends toward the lamp. Auxin, a plant hormone, moves toward the shaded flank. That side elongates faster, so the shoot bends toward the light. Gravity also redirects auxin. It collects on the lower side, making a shoot curve up and a root curve down. The plant steers its growth by moving a chemical signal. Unequal growth on opposite sides makes the bend.

scenes.visual: Start immediately with a lamp at left and an oat shoot. Orange auxin moves toward the shaded right flank; that flank lengthens more, bending the shoot left. Then show a horizontal shoot and root with auxin along each lower side; the shoot curves up and root down. End on the causal chain: auxin redistribution, unequal elongation, bending. Keep the full mechanism visible within the opening spoken passage.

scenes.tts: How does auxin change direction? In Arabidopsis hypocotyls, the seedling stem below the seed leaves, light changes where a carrier called PIN three sits in the cell membrane. Many PIN carriers sit mainly on one face of a cell. Repositioning them steers auxin. A blue-light receptor called phototropin detects the light.

scenes.visual: Zoom into an Arabidopsis hypocotyl cell. Label the blue-light receptor phototropin and the auxin-export carrier PIN3. Move PIN3 carriers to a different membrane face and show orange auxin leaving through that face, redirecting flow toward the shaded flank. Return to faster shaded-side elongation.

scenes.tts: Now lay a seedling on its side. In Arabidopsis root-cap cells, PIN three relocates to the new lower face, redirecting auxin downward. Extra auxin slows elongation on the lower side of the root. The upper side grows faster, so the root curves down. In the shoot, extra auxin speeds elongation on the lower side, so the shoot curves up.

scenes.visual: Rotate an Arabidopsis seedling to horizontal. Inset: root-cap cell with PIN3 relocating to its lower membrane face. Trace auxin toward the lower root flank. Compare root and shoot side by side: lower-root cells elongate less than upper-root cells, producing downward curvature; lower-shoot cells elongate more than upper-shoot cells, producing upward curvature. Label auxin effects separately in each organ.

scenes.tts: The same hormone can act differently in different organs. Plant cells make hormones that change growth, and the signals work together. Auxin helps the growing shoot tip suppress side buds, together with cytokinins and strigolactones. Other hormones control other transitions. Ethylene promotes fruit ripening. Tomatoes engineered to make little ethylene failed to ripen normally. Supplied ethylene restored ripening.

scenes.tts: Light also helps time flowering. Plants use light receptors and a daily clock. In Arabidopsis, a long-day plant, evening light stabilizes the protein CONSTANS. When days are long enough, CONSTANS promotes the gene F T in leaf phloem. F T protein travels to the shoot apex, where flowers form. Leaves read the timing, and a mobile signal carries the message.

scenes.visual: Show an Arabidopsis plant beside a day-night clock. Late-day light coincides with CONSTANS accumulation in a leaf; show FT gene activation in leaf phloem. Track FT protein through the plant to the shoot apex, then show flowers there. Keep the Arabidopsis, long-day plant label visible throughout; do not imply this CONSTANS mechanism applies to every plant.

scenes.tts: Hormones also have opposing effects. Abscisic acid maintains seed dormancy, a state of arrested growth. Gibberellins promote germination. Their effects point in opposite directions: keeping a seed dormant, or starting seedling growth.

scenes.visual: Compare a dormant seed labelled abscisic acid with a germinating seed labelled gibberellins. Use opposing arrows for maintained dormancy and promoted germination. Add no concentrations, timing, or additional molecular pathway.

scenes.tts: Hormones spread defence signals too. Jasmonates signal defence against plant-eating animals. Salicylic acid helps systemic acquired resistance: infection in one part leaves other parts more resistant to later attack. In tobacco, salicylic acid is needed in the distant protected leaves, but is not itself the travelling signal. Jasmonate for insects and salicylic acid for pathogens is a tendency, not a rule.

End card with a compact visual recap in narration order: auxin redistribution and bending; interacting hormones; leaf-to-apex FT signal; dormancy versus germination; defence. No historical experiments or bioassay numbers.
